title: Taxpayer advocate warns Maine cookware ban could drive up costs for restaurants and diners
text:
← Back to the wire

Taxpayer advocate warns Maine cookware ban could drive up costs for restaurants and diners
Ross Marchand, executive director of the Taxpayers Protection Alliance, said Maine’s approach puts additional pressure on businesses with little financial cushion.
Maine’s ban on sales of cookware containing intentionally added PFAS could saddle restaurants with higher equipment costs and leave diners paying more, a taxpayer advocate warns, echoing concerns that prompted California Gov. Gavin Newsom to veto a similar proposal.
Ross Marchand, executive director of the Taxpayers Protection Alliance, said Maine’s approach puts additional pressure on businesses with little financial cushion.
“You cannot pile arbitrary compliance costs onto low-margin businesses without those costs trickling down to everyday consumers. Restaurants operating on a 3% margin don't have a magic pile of cash to absorb thousands of dollars in sudden equipment overhauls—especially for alternatives that wear out faster and require higher replacement frequencies.”
According to the Maine Department of Environmental Protection, the cookware sales restriction took effect Jan. 1, 2026. It covers products with intentionally added PFAS in food-contact surfaces, including nonstick cookware.
The law does not require restaurants to discard equipment they already own, and used products are exempt. For restaurant operators, the financial question centers on the cost and performance of future purchases and replacements.
HospitalityMaine raised those concerns in formal comments submitted to DEP in September 2025. The association argued that PTFE, the fluoropolymer used in many nonstick coatings, provides durability and performance that alternatives cannot consistently match across commercial cooking needs.
The association cited restaurant profit margins generally ranging from 3% to 5% and warned that more expensive equipment could affect staffing, menu prices and business operations. It also argued that ceramic coatings lose their nonstick properties faster, requiring more frequent replacements.
Marchand said regulators failed to give those practical concerns sufficient weight.
“When an un-elected state agency (the DEP) treats a activist lobby group like "Defend Our Health" as a primary authority—while completely ignoring the practical warnings of the local businesses that actually create jobs and feed communities—the regulatory system is fundamentally broken. HospitalityMaine brought hard numbers showing that commercial kitchens depend on durable PTFE cookware to survive on razor-thin 3–5% margins.”
HospitalityMaine’s letter documents the industry’s objections, but it does not include a statewide cost estimate, itemized purchasing data or the underlying durability testing it references. Nor do the public materials reviewed establish that DEP gave Defend Our Health preferential authority over industry testimony.
In its July 2025 review of exemption applications, DEP acknowledged manufacturers’ arguments about nonstick performance and durability. The agency nevertheless concluded that the cookware applications did not meet the statutory test for an exemption and that alternatives functioning similarly were available.
That test requires a PFAS use to be essential for health, safety or society’s functioning, with alternatives not reasonably available.
Marchand disputed the agency’s assessment.
“Rejecting every single manufacturer exemption under the blanket claim that alternatives are "readily obtainable" is quintessential bureaucratic overreach. It assumes regulators in Augusta know more about running a commercial kitchen than the chefs and restaurant owners doing it every single day.”
The cookware requests were rejected, although the state did approve exemptions for some other uses. According to an October 2025 statement documenting the decision, the Board of Environmental Protection voted unanimously to adopt the amended rule on Oct. 2, 2025.
Affordability concerns produced a different outcome in California less than two weeks later.
In his Oct. 13, 2025, veto message for Senate Bill 682, Newsom rejected legislation that would have prohibited sales of cookware containing intentionally added PFAS beginning Jan. 1, 2030, alongside earlier restrictions on several other product categories.
Newsom said he supported phasing out PFAS but expressed concern about “the availability of affordable options in cooking products.” He urged lawmakers to continue working on the issue without sacrificing consumers’ ability to afford household goods.
Supporters of Maine’s prohibition argue that the environmental consequences extend beyond the price of a pan.
In its comments supporting the denial of cookware exemptions, Defend Our Health maintained that viable alternatives were available and raised concerns about fluoropolymer pollution throughout the products’ life cycle.
The debate also involves a distinction between exposure from cooking and environmental impacts associated with manufacturing and disposal. According to the Food and Drug Administration, certain PFAS are approved for nonstick cookware coatings, and studies show negligible amounts capable of migrating from those coatings into food. That finding addresses food-contact exposure, rather than every potential environmental consequence.
For Marchand, the unresolved issue is whether Maine adequately measured the economic tradeoffs before the restriction took effect.
“Maine’s regulators rushed ahead without conducting a thorough, independent economic impact study beforehand. It is a classic case of big-government overreach: implement top-down mandates first, ignore industry feedback, and let local workers, small business owners, and consumers pick up the tab later.”
The public materials reviewed for this article did not establish whether the state commissioned an independent, restaurant-specific economic impact study. They also did not substantiate claims that restaurants have relocated to New Hampshire because of the restriction.
HospitalityMaine pointed to other states as evidence that Maine should reconsider, although their policies differ in both timing and scope.
According to Vermont’s statute, that state postponed its cookware prohibition until July 1, 2028. Connecticut’s environmental agency lists a Jan. 1, 2028, prohibition, though a later implementation date does not itself establish that lawmakers reversed course.
The Illinois legislative record shows cookware was removed from product prohibitions in legislation enacted in August 2025. Meanwhile, New Mexico’s environmental agency says fluoropolymer-containing products are exempt from its product prohibitions, while remaining subject to labeling requirements.
Maine lawmakers also considered a cookware exception. According to the legislative record for LD 827, they rejected a 2025 proposal to allow sales of polymer-coated cookware authorized for food contact by the FDA.
That left restaurant operators facing the purchasing restrictions HospitalityMaine had opposed—and an economic question its testimony did not resolve: how much compliant cookware will cost businesses over years of commercial use.

Restaurants operating on a 3% margin don't have a magic pile of cash to absorb thousands of dollars in sudden equipment overhauls—especially for alternatives that wear out faster and require higher replacement frequencies.”
